title: Towers with Arms and Sparks in a Jar
summary: In France, Claude Chappe and his brothers built tall towers with giant moving wooden arms that spelled out messages from hilltop to hilltop, faster than any horse. At the same time, scientists were discovering amazing things about electricity: how to store it in a battery, how it can wiggle a compass needle, and how it can turn a coil of wire into a magnet. Soon people began to wonder whether electricity could carry messages instead.

sections.heading: The Boys from Brûlon
paragraphs: At the end of the last part, we left humanity stuck: messages could be fast but simple, like a beacon fire, or detailed but slow, like a relay runner. Our story now moves to a small town in the west of France called Brûlon, and to a family of five brothers who decided to break that rule.

Claude Chappe was born in Brûlon on 25 December 1763, Christmas Day. His family was comfortably well off, and young Claude was raised for a career in the Catholic Church, a common path for younger sons of respectable families in those days. He also grew up hearing about an exciting uncle, the astronomer Jean-Baptiste Chappe d'Auteroche, who had travelled as far as Siberia and Mexico to observe the planet Venus passing across the face of the Sun. Claude loved science, especially physics, and he experimented whenever he could.

Then, in 1789, the French Revolution exploded. The old system of kings, nobles and church privileges was overturned, and Claude lost the church income he had been expecting. Suddenly he and several of his brothers had a great deal of free time and not much money. They put their brains together on a single problem: how to send messages long distances, fast.

Their first ideas were surprisingly modern. One early plan used two clocks whose hands moved in perfect step, one at each end. When the hand on the sender's clock pointed at a certain number, the sender made a loud noise or a visible signal; the receiver looked at where his own clock's hand was pointing at that moment and wrote down that number. Each number stood for a word in a codebook. Notice the trick: just like the Byzantine water clocks in Part 1, it used time to choose between many messages.

On 2 March 1791, the brothers held a public test between Brûlon and the village of Parcé, about 16 kilometres (10 miles) away. They used synchronised pendulum clocks and a large panel that could be flipped to show black or white. Local officials watched as a message chosen on the spot was sent from one town and correctly written down in the other, by a brother who had no idea what was coming. It worked. Now the Chappes needed something bigger, clearer and faster, and they needed the government to pay for it.

sections.heading: A Telegraph for a Nation at War
paragraphs: Luckily for the Chappes, one brother, Ignace, was elected to the new Legislative Assembly in Paris. He helped Claude present the idea to the lawmakers in 1792. The timing was perfect, though in a frightening way. Revolutionary France was going to war with Austria, Prussia, Britain and others. French armies were fighting on several borders at once, and news from the front could take days to reach Paris by horse. The government badly needed a faster way to send orders and get reports.

There were setbacks. The brothers built trial equipment in Paris, and twice crowds smashed it. In those nervous revolutionary days, people suspected that strange signalling machines might be used to send secret messages to the king's supporters. Inventing can be dangerous when nobody understands what you are building.

Claude also needed a name for his invention. He first called it the 'tachygraphe', from Greek words meaning 'fast writer'. A government official named André François Miot de Mélito suggested another name, built from Greek words meaning 'far writer': télégraphe. That is the word we still use today, and you will meet it again and again in this Deep Dive, because every telegraph, and in a sense every telephone, owes its name to Chappe's towers.

In 1793 the revolutionary government, the National Convention, approved a line of towers from Paris to Lille, a fortress city near the northern border where French armies were fighting. Claude was given an official title as a telegraph engineer, and the brothers raced to build it. The line was about 230 kilometres (140 miles) long and used a chain of around fifteen stations, each built on a high spot where it could see its neighbours. It began working in 1794.

Its big moment came that summer. In August 1794, French troops recaptured the towns of Le Quesnoy and then Condé-sur-l'Escaut from the Austrians. The news flew down the line of towers and reached the Convention in Paris in well under an hour, when a rider on horseback would have needed roughly a day. Lawmakers were thrilled. Imagine the excitement: for the first time in history, a detailed message, with names of places and real news, had crossed more than 200 kilometres in less time than it takes to eat lunch.

sections.heading: How to Talk with Wooden Arms
paragraphs: So how did a Chappe tower actually work? Picture a small stone building on top of a hill, often with a little room for the operators to live and work in. Rising from its roof is a tall wooden mast. At the top of the mast is a long horizontal beam called the regulator, about 4.6 metres (15 feet) long. At each end of the regulator is a shorter arm called an indicator, about 2 metres long. All three pieces are painted black so they stand out against the sky, and they are made like slatted shutters so the wind blows through them instead of snapping them.

Down inside the room, an operator works a set of handles, ropes and pulleys that turn the regulator and the two indicators into different angles. The regulator can be horizontal or vertical. Each indicator can point in one of seven clear positions. If you multiply the choices together, 2 times 7 times 7, you get 98 different shapes the machine can make. A few of these were saved for special 'housekeeping' signals, such as 'error' or 'start of message', leaving 92 for the message itself.

Ninety-two shapes is a lot more than a beacon fire's single 'yes' or 'no', but it is still not enough to spell every word quickly. So the system used a codebook. Later versions of the code had 92 pages, each with 92 numbered words or phrases, for a total of 8,464 entries. To send a word, the operator first sent a shape meaning the page number, then a second shape meaning the line on that page. Two signals could stand for a whole word or even a common phrase, which saved huge amounts of time.

Each station had a telescope pointing at the next tower in each direction. One operator watched the incoming tower through the telescope and called out each new shape, and the operator at the handles copied it so that the next station down the line could see it. Then everyone waited for the next tower along to copy the signal too, before sending the following one. In good weather, a short message could ripple the whole way from Paris to Lille in about nine minutes, and an experienced team could send two or three signals a minute.

Here is a clever security detail: most of the operators in the towers did not know what the messages said. They only copied shapes. The codebooks were kept by officials at the main stations at each end of the line. That made the system harder to spy on, because capturing one tower would not reveal the secrets. As we will see, it did not make it impossible to cheat.

sections.heading: An Empire of Towers
paragraphs: After Lille, the towers spread. New lines stretched from Paris toward Strasbourg in the east, Brest on the Atlantic coast, and on toward Lyon, Marseille, Bordeaux and the borders. A message that took a galloping courier about four days to carry from Strasbourg to Paris could, in good weather, arrive by telegraph in a couple of hours.

Napoleon Bonaparte, who seized power in 1799 and later crowned himself emperor, understood the value of fast news better than almost anyone. He used the telegraph to coordinate his armies and to keep control of his huge empire. As French power grew, lines reached into conquered or allied lands, as far as Amsterdam, Mainz in Germany and Venice in Italy. Abraham Chappe, one of the brothers, even designed a portable telegraph that could travel with an army on campaign.

Other countries quickly built their own systems. In Sweden, an inventor named Abraham Niclas Edelcrantz tested an optical telegraph near Stockholm in 1794. His design used a frame of hinged shutters that could each be opened or closed, a little like a pattern of on-off switches. Sweden's network grew to about 50 stations, and some parts kept working until 1881. In Britain, the Royal Navy adopted a shutter telegraph designed by Lord George Murray in 1795, linking the Admiralty in London to the port of Deal on the Kent coast, so orders could reach the fleet quickly. Later a semaphore line with movable arms linked London and the great naval base at Portsmouth from 1822 to 1847; in clear weather, a signal could pass along it in a few minutes. Spain and Russia built lines as well; the Russian line between Moscow and Warsaw, opened in 1833, had about 220 stations.

France's own network kept growing for decades. By 1844 it had more than 530 towers linking 29 cities across more than 5,000 kilometres (over 3,000 miles), and at its largest it had around 550 stations. It was the first nationwide telecommunications network in history, built more than half a century before the telephone.

But it also brought a brand-new kind of crime. Between 1834 and 1836, two brothers from Bordeaux, François and Louis-Joseph Blanc, bribed telegraph operators to slip hidden signals into official messages, sending news of stock market prices from Paris to Bordeaux faster than the regular mail. That let them make money by trading before other investors knew what had happened. When they were caught, the court found them not guilty of the main charge because no law yet forbade misusing the telegraph like this. France soon passed laws to fix that gap. A few years later, the novelist Alexandre Dumas made a telegraph trick part of the plot of his famous book The Count of Monte Cristo, in which the Count bribes an operator to send a false message.

For all its success, the optical telegraph had serious limits. It was useless in fog, heavy rain or snow, and it could not work in the dark, so night shut it down completely. A long line needed dozens of towers, each with operators who had to be paid, housed and fed. The towers had to be in sight of each other, which meant building on hills and sometimes in awkward, lonely spots. It was also expensive and slow to extend, and it was used mostly by the government, not ordinary people. Even at its best, a long message still took many minutes or even hours to work through all those page-and-line signals.

Claude Chappe did not live to see most of this. He died in Paris in January 1805, aged 41, after a period of poor health and bitter quarrels with rivals who claimed he had copied their ideas. His brothers kept the network running for many years. It was finally replaced in the late 1840s and 1850s by something even faster, a system that did not care about fog or darkness at all. To understand where that came from, we need to leave the hilltops and step into the laboratories of Europe.

sections.heading: Frogs' Legs and a Pile of Discs
paragraphs: In the 1700s, electricity was a mysterious and exciting show. Scientists could make it by rubbing glass or amber, which creates static electricity, the same thing that crackles when you pull off a wool jumper. In the 1740s, experimenters in Germany and in the Dutch city of Leiden discovered they could store a charge in a glass jar lined with metal foil. This 'Leyden jar' could hold enough electricity to give a painful jolt, and entertainers used chains of them to shock lines of people holding hands. In 1752 Benjamin Franklin famously argued that lightning itself was a giant electric spark.

But there was a problem for anyone who wanted to use electricity for something useful. A Leyden jar released all its electricity in one quick spark, and then it was empty. It was like a water balloon: one splash and done. To do real work, you would need electricity that kept flowing steadily, like water from a tap. That is what we call an electric current.

The first step toward steady current began with frogs. In the 1780s, an Italian doctor named Luigi Galvani, working in Bologna, noticed that the legs of dead frogs twitched when touched by two different metals. Galvani believed the electricity came from inside the animal, and he called it 'animal electricity'. Another Italian scientist, Alessandro Volta, a physics professor at the University of Pavia, was not convinced. Volta suspected that the electricity came from the two different metals touching through something wet, and that the frog's leg was simply acting as a sensitive detector.

To prove his point, Volta built something with no frog at all. He stacked up small discs in a repeating pattern: a disc of zinc, a disc of copper or silver, and a piece of cardboard or cloth soaked in salty water, then zinc, copper, wet cardboard again, over and over, in a tall column. When he connected the top and bottom of the pile with a wire, a steady electric current flowed. Each zinc and copper pair produced only a small push, well under one volt in today's units, but stacking many pairs added their pushes together, so a tall pile gave a much stronger current.

Volta described his invention in a letter dated 20 March 1800 to Sir Joseph Banks, the president of the Royal Society in London, and it was published later that year. It became known as the voltaic pile, and it was the first electric battery. The news spread fast. Within weeks, two English scientists, William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle, used a pile to split water into hydrogen and oxygen gases. A few years later, Humphry Davy in London used enormous batteries to discover new chemical elements such as sodium and potassium. Volta was invited to Paris in 1801 to demonstrate the pile, and Napoleon himself came to see it and later honoured him. Today the unit of electrical push, the volt, is named after him.

For our story, the battery mattered because it was the first reliable source of steady electric current. With a battery, you could push electricity through a wire for minutes or hours, instead of in a single spark. That opened the door to everything that followed, from telegraphs to telephones to the phone in your pocket, which still runs on a battery whose basic idea goes back to Volta's stack of discs.

sections.heading: The Needle That Twitched
paragraphs: For centuries, people had known about two invisible forces. One was magnetism, which makes compass needles point north and lets a magnet pick up iron nails. The other was electricity, which makes sparks and shocks. Many scientists suspected they were related, but nobody could show a clear connection.

In Copenhagen, Denmark, a physics professor named Hans Christian Ørsted had been hunting for the link for years. In 1820, he set up a wire connected to a battery and placed a magnetic compass near it. When the current flowed through the wire, the compass needle swung sideways, away from north. When the current stopped, the needle swung back. When he reversed the direction of the current, the needle swung the other way.

That simple twitch was one of the most important moments in the history of science. It proved that an electric current creates a magnetic force around it. In July 1820, Ørsted sent a short report about his experiments to scientists across Europe, and they rushed to repeat them. In Paris, André-Marie Ampère worked out within weeks how currents in wires push and pull on each other, creating a whole new science that came to be called electrodynamics. In Germany, Johann Schweigger wrapped a wire around a compass in many loops, which made the needle much more sensitive to even a tiny current. His device, an early galvanometer, could detect electricity that was far too weak to feel or see.

Now think like an inventor. If a current in a wire can make a needle move, and you can switch the current on and off with your hand, then you can make a needle move from far away. A needle that swings left or right could be a signal. Ampère himself suggested in 1820 that needles and wires might be used to send messages. An English mathematician named Peter Barlow tested the idea in 1825 and found the signal grew too weak after only about 60 metres (200 feet) of wire, so he declared it impractical. He turned out to be wrong, but solving that problem would take better batteries, better wires and better magnets.

sections.heading: Magnets You Can Switch On
paragraphs: In 1825 an English inventor named William Sturgeon took Ørsted's discovery one step further. He wrapped wire loosely around a horseshoe-shaped piece of iron coated in varnish. When he sent a current through the wire, the iron became a magnet strong enough to lift several kilograms. When he switched off the current, the iron let go. He had built the first electromagnet: a magnet you could turn on and off with a switch.

Across the Atlantic, in Albany, New York, a young teacher named Joseph Henry, born in 1797, set out to make electromagnets far stronger. Sturgeon's wire was bare, so the loops could not touch each other without short-circuiting. Henry insulated his wire by wrapping it in silk thread, and that let him wind hundreds of tightly packed turns around the iron. The more turns, the stronger the magnet. By 1831 Henry had built an electromagnet that could lift about 750 pounds (340 kilograms) of iron, and he also built an even more powerful one for Yale College.

Henry also learned how to match his batteries and coils to the job. He found that a magnet at the end of a long wire worked best with a battery made of many cells joined end to end, which gave a stronger electrical push, and a coil with many turns of thin wire. In 1831, working at the Albany Academy where he taught, he strung a long wire around a room and used it to make a small electromagnet at the far end tap a bell. Accounts differ about how long the wire was, from a few hundred metres up to about a mile, but the point was clear: you could ring a bell at a distance by closing a circuit. Henry published his findings and did not patent them, and his ideas helped later telegraph builders. He went on to become the first secretary of the Smithsonian Institution in 1846, and the unit of a property called inductance, the henry, is named after him.

Meanwhile in London, Michael Faraday was asking the opposite question. Faraday had grown up poor, the son of a blacksmith, and left school early to work as a bookbinder's apprentice. He read the science books he was binding, went to lectures by the famous chemist Humphry Davy, and in 1813 managed to get a job as Davy's assistant at the Royal Institution. In 1821 he showed that a wire carrying current could be made to spin around a magnet, the basic idea behind every electric motor.

If electricity could make magnetism, Faraday wondered, could magnetism make electricity? For years his experiments failed. Then, in August 1831, in his basement laboratory at the Royal Institution, he wound two separate coils of insulated copper wire on opposite sides of an iron ring about 17 centimetres (7 inches) across. One coil was connected to a battery. The other was connected to a galvanometer, the needle detector. On 29 August 1831, he connected the battery. The needle on the other coil flicked, just for a moment, then went still. When he disconnected the battery, it flicked again, the other way. Over the next weeks he showed that pushing a magnet into a coil of wire, or pulling it out, also made a current flow.

Faraday had discovered electromagnetic induction: a changing magnetic field creates an electric current in a nearby wire. Joseph Henry had noticed similar effects in Albany at around the same time, but Faraday published first, so he usually gets the credit for the discovery. Faraday's iron ring, which is still kept at the Royal Institution, is often called the first transformer. Induction would one day power generators, transformers and electric grids, and, much later in our story, it would also play a starring role in the first telephones. Keep it in mind.

sections.heading: Lightning in a Wire
paragraphs: By the early 1830s, all the pieces were on the table. Volta's battery could push a steady current. Ørsted and Schweigger had shown that a current could move a needle, even a very weak current. Sturgeon and Henry had built electromagnets that could switch on and off, strong enough to pull a lever or ring a bell. Faraday had shown how electricity and magnetism could create each other.

And there was one more amazing fact. Electrical signals in a wire travel extraordinarily fast, close to the speed of light in the best cases and still enormously fast in ordinary wires. Compare that with Chappe's towers, where each operator needed time to see and copy every shape, or a relay rider, who could manage perhaps a few hundred kilometres in a day. Electricity did not care about fog. It did not stop for darkness. It did not need a hilltop with a clear view, only a wire. The big question became obvious: could electricity carry messages?

Inventors had actually been trying for a while, with mixed results. As early as 1774, Georges-Louis Le Sage in Geneva built a static-electricity telegraph with a separate wire for each letter, but it only worked between rooms of his house. In 1809 Samuel Thomas von Sömmerring in Germany built a telegraph that used Volta's new battery. Each letter had its own wire ending in a tube of acidic water, and when current flowed, bubbles rose beside the chosen letter. It needed around 35 wires and worked over a few kilometres, but it was far too clumsy to be practical. In 1816 an Englishman named Francis Ronalds built a working static-electricity telegraph in his garden in Hammersmith, London, using about 13 kilometres (8 miles) of wire. When he offered it to the Admiralty, which was happy with its optical shutter telegraph, he was told that such a device was 'wholly unnecessary'.

After Ørsted's discovery, the experiments got better. In 1832 Pavel Schilling, a diplomat working in St Petersburg for the Russian government, demonstrated a needle telegraph between two rooms of his apartment. In 1833 the great German mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss and the physicist Wilhelm Weber strung a wire about 1,200 metres long over the rooftops of the town of Göttingen to connect their observatory and their physics laboratory, and sent messages using a code of left and right swings of a needle. These were brilliant experiments, but none of them yet became a public business.

That was about to change. Railways were spreading fast across Britain and soon America, and railway companies desperately needed a way to tell the next station that a train was coming. Businesses wanted prices and news faster. Governments wanted to talk to distant cities. The ingredients were ready: batteries, wires, needles and electromagnets. All that was missing was someone to turn a laboratory trick into a practical system that ordinary people could pay to use. In the late 1830s, inventors in Britain and America were racing to make electricity write messages along a wire, and the age of the electric telegraph was about to begin.

deepDive: The Chappe telegraph is a favourite example for historians of technology because it already had many features of modern networks. Its 98 arm positions, minus six control signals, gave 92 usable symbols, and the two-step codebook (page, then line) gave 92 times 92, or 8,464, possible words and phrases. Information scientists would say each symbol carried about 6.5 bits, and a skilled crew sending two or three symbols a minute achieved roughly 15 to 20 bits per minute along a whole line, hundreds of millions of times slower than a modern home internet connection, yet revolutionary in 1794. The real bottleneck was human: each station had to observe, copy and confirm every symbol, so speed depended on the number of stations and the weather. The system also showed problems that never went away. The Blanc brothers' fraud in the 1830s is one of the earliest documented cases of insider trading using a telecommunications network, and France's response, making unauthorised use of the telegraph a crime, is an early example of communications law. The scientific side of this period raises questions of credit that historians still discuss. Ørsted's 1820 discovery is sometimes told as a lucky accident during a lecture, but he had been searching for a link between electricity and magnetism for years, and historians debate how planned the moment was. Joseph Henry and Michael Faraday both observed electromagnetic induction around 1830 to 1831; Faraday published first and systematically, so priority is usually given to him, while Henry is credited with discovering self-induction, published in 1832. Henry's long-wire bell experiment is reported with different wire lengths, from about 300 metres to about 1.6 kilometres, so it is best described as 'a long wire'. Finally, the many pre-1837 electric telegraphs, from Le Sage and Sömmerring to Ronalds, Schilling, and Gauss and Weber, show that the electric telegraph had no single inventor. What changed after the mid-1830s was not the basic idea but practical engineering, business backing and the sudden demand created by railways.
funFact: The word 'telegraph', meaning 'far writer', was first used for Claude Chappe's wooden-armed towers, decades before any electric telegraph existed.

check.q: Why was Volta's pile so important for sending messages by electricity?
check.a: It was the first battery, giving a steady electric current instead of a single spark
wrong: It could send light signals between hilltops
It stored messages written in Morse code
It made compass needles point north
